parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman books a river cruise for a celebration.
script: Good morning, Riverline Cruises, Martin speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book a private cruise for a party.
Lovely. Can I take your name?
Joanne Kerr. K, E, double R.
It's a graduation celebration for my daughter and her friends.
Congratulations! What date are you thinking of?
Then the best boat would be the Kingfisher. K, I, N, G, F, I, S, H, E, R. It holds up to fifty people.
From Westgate Pier, which is about five minutes' walk from the station.
Our evening cruises last three hours.
We offer either a cold buffet or a barbecue on the upper deck. In July, most people choose the barbecue.
The barbecue, then. How much does it cost?
Thirty-eight pounds per head, including the food and soft drinks.
Yes, there's a sound system, and you're welcome to bring your own DJ.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: An organiser describes the programme for a science festival.
script: Hello everyone, and thanks for coming. I'm Fiona, the director of this year's City Science Festival.
The theme this year is water: everything from the oceans to the water in our bodies.
Almost all the events are free. The only exception is the laser show, for which tickets cost five pounds.
You don't need to book for talks, but the hands-on workshops have limited places, so please book those online.
Something completely new this year is a late-night event at the museum, open until eleven p.m., with music and science demonstrations for adults.
Let me tell you where some of the main events will be. The robot competition, where school teams build robots that swim, takes place at the university.
The laser show is in the cathedral. The effect of the lights on the old stone walls is spectacular.
The rock-pool safari, exploring creatures on the shore, starts from the harbour.
Science storytelling for young children will be held in the central library.
Kite-making, to learn about wind and air pressure, will be in the park, weather permitting.
And the talk on deep-sea creatures will take place in the museum's main hall.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A student, Tasnim, discusses her essay plan with her tutor, Dr Webb.
script: Hello Tasnim. Let's look at your essay plan on urban migration.
Thanks. My focus is why people move from rural areas to Dhaka, rather than what happens after they arrive.
That's a sensible focus. My main concern is the structure. At the moment, the argument jumps between ideas. You need a clearer order.
I'll reorganise it around the main causes.
Also, some of your population figures are quite old. You should use the 2022 census data, which is now available.
OK. For my case study, I was going to look at garment workers. Most of them are migrants from rural areas.
That works well. And remember, the word limit is three thousand words.
Right. Could you comment on my sources?
Of course. The World Bank report is excellent. It's recent and very detailed.
It's useful, but it was published in 2005, so it's rather old.
What about the blog by the NGO?
It has interesting stories, but it isn't an academic source. Use it carefully.
Remember it's designed to present the government positively, so it may be biased. And the encyclopedia article is too general for this level.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the road network of the Inca Empire.
script: Today we're going to look at one of the greatest engineering achievements of the ancient Americas: the road network of the Inca Empire.

At its height, in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, the empire stretched along the Andes mountains, and it was connected by a network of roads around forty thousand kilometres long. The Inca called it the Qhapaq Nan, spelled N, A, N, which means the royal road.

The Inca had no wheeled vehicles and no horses, so the roads were used by people on foot. Messages were carried by runners called chasqui, who worked in relays. Each ran a short distance and passed the message to the next, and together they could cover around two hundred and forty kilometres in a day.
The Inca did not have writing as we know it. Instead, information such as numbers and accounts was recorded on knotted cords called quipu, spelled Q, U, I, P, U.
Along the roads, there were rest houses called tambos, where travellers could find food and shelter, and where supplies were stored.
To cross deep gorges, the Inca built rope bridges made from woven grass. One of these, the Q'eswachaka bridge in Peru, is still rebuilt every year by local communities using traditional methods.
The roads were used by armies, officials and caravans of llamas, which carried goods across the empire.
In 2014, the road network was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, shared by six countries.
Ironically, when the Spanish arrived in the 1530s, the excellent roads helped them to invade the empire quickly.

passages.title: The Taj Mahal
paragraphs: The Taj Mahal, on the banks of the Yamuna River in Agra, is one of the most famous buildings in the world. It was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 while giving birth to their fourteenth child. According to contemporary accounts, the emperor was so grief-stricken that his hair turned grey within months.

Construction began soon after her death and continued for more than twenty years, with the main tomb completed first and the surrounding buildings and gardens finished around 1653. Historians estimate that around 20,000 workers were involved, including stonecutters, masons, calligraphers and inlay specialists, some of whom came from Persia and Central Asia.

The tomb is built mainly of white marble brought from Makrana in Rajasthan, more than 300 kilometres away. Its walls are decorated with a technique known as pietra dura, in which semi-precious stones such as jade, lapis lazuli and carnelian are cut and fitted into the marble to form flowers and patterns. Passages from the Quran are inscribed in black marble around the arches, with the letters cleverly enlarged towards the top so that they appear the same size when viewed from below.

The building's design reflects careful planning. The four minarets at the corners of the platform lean very slightly outwards. This was deliberate: in the event of an earthquake, they would fall away from the central tomb rather than onto it.

Shah Jahan's final years were unhappy. In 1658, he was deposed by his son Aurangzeb and imprisoned in Agra Fort, from where, according to tradition, he could see the Taj Mahal across the river. When he died in 1666, he was buried beside his wife.

Today, the Taj Mahal faces new threats. Air pollution from traffic and industry has caused the white marble to turn yellow, and insects breeding in the polluted river leave marks on the walls. To protect it, the Indian government created a zone around the monument, known as the Taj Trapezium Zone, where polluting industries are restricted. The marble is periodically cleaned with a traditional clay mud pack, which draws out dirt without damaging the stone.

passages.title: Plagues of Locusts
paragraphs: Most of the time, desert locusts are solitary insects, living quietly in the deserts of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia and avoiding one another. But when heavy rains produce plenty of vegetation and their numbers grow, crowded together, they undergo a dramatic transformation. In a 2009 study, scientists showed that when locusts are crowded, their nervous systems release more serotonin, a chemical that triggers the change. They switch to a 'gregarious' phase, changing colour, becoming more active and seeking out each other's company.

Gregarious locusts can form enormous swarms. A single square kilometre of swarm may contain up to 80 million insects, and each locust can eat roughly its own weight in fresh food every day. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization, a swarm of one square kilometre can eat as much food in a day as about 35,000 people. Swarms can travel more than 100 kilometres a day with the wind.

Between 2019 and 2020, East Africa and South Asia experienced one of the worst locust upsurges in decades. Its origins lay in unusual cyclones that brought heavy rain to remote deserts in the Arabian Peninsula, creating ideal breeding conditions. Swarms spread into the Horn of Africa, and Kenya suffered its worst outbreak in 70 years, threatening the food supplies of millions of people.

Preventing such disasters depends on monitoring. The Food and Agriculture Organization runs a Desert Locust Information Service, which uses satellite data on rainfall and vegetation to predict where locusts are likely to breed. Field officers in affected countries record observations using an app called eLocust3, which sends data directly to the central forecasting system.

When swarms do form, the most common response is spraying chemical pesticides, often from aircraft. These are effective but can harm other insects, wildlife and people. An alternative is a biopesticide based on a fungus called Metarhizium, which infects and kills locusts but is harmless to most other animals. It works more slowly, however, so it is best used against young locusts before swarms become large.

Scientists warn that climate change may make outbreaks more frequent. Warmer seas are associated with more intense cyclones in the Indian Ocean, which can bring rain to deserts and trigger breeding. Most experts agree that the key to controlling locusts is early detection: stopping outbreaks while they are still small is far cheaper and less harmful than fighting swarms once they have formed.

passages.title: AI and Homework
paragraphs: Since powerful AI chatbots became freely available at the end of 2022, students around the world have been using them to help with homework, from solving maths problems to writing essays. Many teachers have reacted with alarm, fearing that students will use the tools to cheat and, in doing so, fail to develop essential skills.

There is evidence that these fears are not unfounded. In a study carried out in high schools in Turkey, some students practised maths with access to a standard AI chatbot, while others practised without it. The students using the chatbot did much better during practice sessions, but when the tool was taken away for the exam, they performed worse than students who had never used it. Many had simply asked the chatbot for answers. In my view, this shows clearly that students who use AI without restrictions may learn less.

Interestingly, the same study tested a second version of the chatbot, designed to act as a tutor. Instead of giving answers, it offered hints and encouraged students to work through problems themselves. Students using this version did not suffer the same drop in exam performance, suggesting that the design of the tool, and how it is used, makes a great difference.

Some schools have responded by trying to detect AI-generated work. However, detection tools have proved unreliable. A study at Stanford University found that several popular detectors frequently misjudged essays written by people who were not native speakers of English, labelling their genuine work as AI-generated. False accusations of cheating can be deeply damaging to students.

It is also important to recognise the benefits. Used well, AI tools can explain difficult ideas in different ways, give instant feedback on drafts and help students who are learning in a second language to understand complex texts. For students without access to private tutors, such support could be particularly valuable.

I believe that banning AI tools is neither practical nor desirable. Instead, schools should change how they assess learning, making greater use of writing done in class, oral exams and presentations, which make it much harder to rely on AI. At the same time, students should be taught when and how to use AI appropriately, as a tool that supports their thinking rather than one that replaces it.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the average number of daily flights at one airport between 2000 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The line graph shows the average number of international, domestic and cargo flights operating each day at one airport between 2000 and 2024.

Overall, international and cargo flights increased steadily over the period, while domestic flights rose at first and then declined. As a result, international flights replaced domestic flights as the most common type.

In 2000, domestic flights were the most numerous, at 220 a day, compared with 150 international flights and just 30 cargo flights. Domestic flights increased to a peak of 260 in 2006, but then fell gradually, reaching 180 in 2024.

International flights, meanwhile, grew continuously. They overtook domestic flights between 2006 and 2012, when they reached 250 a day, and rose to 380 by 2024, more than double their original level. Cargo flights also increased throughout the period, more than doubling from 30 to 75 a day, although they remained by far the smallest category.

task2.text: Some people think it is important to preserve traditional skills, such as handicrafts and traditional farming methods. Others believe that young people should focus on learning modern skills. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: In a rapidly changing world, young people face pressure to learn skills that will help them find jobs in modern industries. At the same time, many traditional crafts and practices are disappearing. In my view, modern skills should be the priority for most young people, but traditional skills are also valuable and deserve active protection.

Those who emphasise modern skills make a strong practical case. Jobs in technology, healthcare and engineering are growing, and they usually offer better pay and security than traditional crafts. Digital literacy, in particular, has become essential in almost every type of work. Young people have limited time for education, so it makes sense for them to focus on skills that will help them support themselves and their families.

However, traditional skills have value that goes beyond economics. Crafts such as weaving, pottery and woodcarving are part of a community's cultural identity, and once the knowledge is lost, it may be impossible to recover. Some traditional skills are also highly relevant today. Traditional farming methods, for example, often protect soil and water better than intensive modern agriculture, and handmade products can find markets among tourists and buyers who value sustainability and authenticity. In Bangladesh, for instance, traditional nakshi kantha embroidery provides income for many rural women.

In my opinion, the two approaches can be combined. Schools should prepare young people for modern careers, but governments and communities should also support traditional skills through apprenticeships, museums and fair-trade markets. Technology can even help, for example by allowing craftspeople to sell their work online.

In conclusion, although modern skills are essential for most young people's futures, I believe traditional skills should also be preserved, because they contain cultural and practical knowledge that society cannot afford to lose.

speaking.cue:
Describe a river or lake that you have visited.
You should say:
- where it is
- when you went there
- what you did there
and explain why you remember it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about Kaptai Lake, in the Rangamati hills in south-east Bangladesh, which I visited with my family about two years ago. It's actually an artificial lake, created in the nineteen-sixties when a dam was built on the Karnaphuli River, and it's the largest lake in the country. The scenery is beautiful. The lake is surrounded by green hills, and there are lots of small islands. We hired a wooden boat for the whole day and travelled across the lake. We stopped at a hanging bridge, which is a popular spot for photos, and then visited a village where people from one of the indigenous communities sell handwoven cloth. My mother bought a shawl there. For lunch, we ate at a small restaurant on an island, where we had fresh fish from the lake cooked with bamboo shoots, which I'd never tried before. I remember it because it was so peaceful. Being on the water, with only the sound of the boat engine and the birds, felt completely different from the noise of the city. I also learned that when the lake was created, many local people lost their homes and land, which made me think about the hidden costs of development.
